research.topic: Curiosity discovers a field of Martian honeycomb textures

facts.text: Curiosity found a field of honeycomb-shaped polygons across Valle Grande.
Individual polygons measure about 1.5 to 3 inches across.
Some polygons may be ancient mud cracks while others may have formed as buried water moved through soil.

concepts.headline: Mars has a honeycomb floor
concepts.premise: Curiosity found a valley covered in tiny polygons with more than one possible origin.
concepts.whyItWorks: A huge alien valley is reduced to a familiar floor pattern.
concepts.takeaway: Scientists are testing the chemistry now.
concepts.punchline: Mars has officially entered its floor-tile era.
storyMoves: Reveal the huge valley covered in an unexpected repeating pattern.
Escalate by showing that every tile is only inches wide.
Reveal two possible water-driven origins for the same visible pattern.
Resolve on the planetary view and reframe Mars as a tiled floor.

concepts.headline: Mars may have dried mud under its wheels
concepts.premise: Some tiny polygons could preserve ancient wet conditions.
concepts.whyItWorks: The visual starts ordinary and ends planetary.
concepts.takeaway: The cracks may preserve evidence of ancient wet conditions.
concepts.punchline: Mars kept the receipt from mud season.
storyMoves: Open on a valley whose surface looks strangely familiar.
Move close enough to reveal inch-wide cracks rather than rocks.
Connect those cracks to ancient wet conditions scientists are testing.
Return wide and land the mud-season punchline.

concepts.headline: Buried water may have drawn shapes in Martian soil
concepts.premise: Mineral-rich water could have squeezed through buried sediment.
concepts.whyItWorks: Invisible movement becomes a visible pattern.
concepts.takeaway: Buried water may have shaped the Martian soil.
concepts.punchline: Even Martian plumbing leaves a pattern.
storyMoves: Show the unexplained field of shapes across the valley.
Escalate with the small repeating pattern visible up close.
Reveal that buried water may have drawn the shapes through soil.
Resolve on the landscape with the Martian-plumbing joke.

concepts.headline: A giant Martian field is made of tiny shapes
concepts.premise: The largest field of these textures seen by Curiosity contains inch-wide pieces.
concepts.whyItWorks: The scale reversal is instantly visual.
concepts.takeaway: Curiosity found its largest field of these textures.
concepts.punchline: Mars went big by building very small.
storyMoves: Begin with the largest field of these textures Curiosity has seen.
Contrast the giant landscape with shapes only inches across.
Reveal the possible ancient-water process behind the tiny pieces.
Resolve by returning to the giant landscape for the scale joke.

concepts.headline: NASA found the pattern before the explanation
concepts.premise: Scientists still need chemistry tests to separate two possible origins.
concepts.whyItWorks: The mystery stays open after the reveal.
concepts.takeaway: Chemistry tests must distinguish between the two origins.
concepts.punchline: The floor is ready. The label is pending.
storyMoves: Open on the strange finished-looking pattern scientists found.
Escalate with two plausible origins that look identical from above.
Reveal that chemistry testing is needed to separate the explanations.
Resolve on the landscape while the label remains pending.

selection.reason: It has the clearest visual scale change and shortest deadpan payoff.

beats: Breaking news. From Mars, Curiosity just found a sea of tiny honeycomb shapes stretching across an entire valley.
Each polygon is only a few inches wide.
Some may be ancient mud cracks. Others could have formed when buried water squeezed through the soil.
Scientists are testing the chemistry now. Mars has officially entered its floor-tile era.
